title: Godot's own log filled C: with unbounded error spam
impact: ~10 GB across 5 files in %APPDATA%/Godot/app_userdata, re-created every run; five concurrent agents each burned ~2 GB
cause: Godot's log rotates at 2 GB per file with no total ceiling (max_log_files=5), and debug/file_logging/enable_file_logging in project.godot does NOT disable it because the engine reads the .pc variant, which stays true. A mind_cultivation test entered an unbounded retry loop and push_error fired on every iteration.
guard: tools/godot.py passes --log-file (inserted before the bare --, or Godot treats it as a project arg and keeps writing to the profile), plus LOG_BYTE_CEILING and a silence ceiling. TestCase kills the process via OS.crash past MAX_FAILURES/MAX_ASSERTIONS so a looping test body stops.

title: A tests/ui run exhausted RAM and forced a power-cycle
impact: 67 GB resident / 105 GB commit at ~0.3 GB/s; the 96 GB machine stopped responding and was power-cycled twice
cause: Two independent defects. (1) queue_free() defers to end-of-frame, and the headless runner drives every test from SceneTree._initialize(), which returns before the first frame, so a deferred free NEVER runs: ScreenStack.pop() orphaned a screen subtree per navigation and WorldMapScreen._clear_graph() stacked a fresh map graph per refresh. (2) `while count < board.size() + 4` where the body inserts one key per pass never terminates, because size grows in lockstep with count, allocating a nested Dictionary per pass.
guard: test_no_deferred_free.gd fails the build on any queue_free() in res://src (no exemptions); ScreenStack.pop() and _clear_graph() detach then free(); both self-growing loops snapshot the bound before the loop; RAM_CEILING_BYTES in tools/godot.py kills a run at 12 GB and names the cause.

title: A bulk revert destroyed another agent's uncommitted work
impact: Another agent's finished work was lost and could not be recovered: uncommitted work has no reflog entry
cause: The working tree is shared with live agents. A path-less `git checkout .` / `git restore .` / `git stash`, or a blanket `git add -A` / `git commit -a`, is not 'reverting my files' -- it reverts everyone's. This happened twice.
guard: AGENTS.md workflow rule 8 forbids path-less checkout/restore/stash and force-push; rule 7 requires staging only your own paths and committing per vertical slice. Enforcement is by review, not by tools, so it is mitigated rather than resolved.

title: A run invoked Godot DIRECTLY, bypassing tools/godot.py, so no RAM ceiling applied at all and the machine was reset
impact: The machine was power-cycled once by an agent force-killing the runaway, and reset by the OS later, destroying all in-flight agent sessions. No committed work was lost, but every uncommitted change and every running agent was.
cause: tools/godot.py owns the log, RAM and clock ceilings AND the --log-file redirection. Invoking the Godot binary directly - which is exactly what a probe or a hand-typed command does - gets none of them, so a run with no output at all passes every ceiling by producing nothing measurable. A res://tests/_probe_ui_mem.gd run reached 73 GB resident climbing at ~8.2 GB per 20 s with roughly three minutes of headroom on a 95 GB machine. The identical signature recurred on relaunch (16 GB to 23 GB in 20 s). A later run of the same class of shape exhausted RAM hard enough that the PC reset and every live agent session was lost.
guard: AGENTS.md forbids invoking Godot, gdformat or gdlint directly and requires every entrypoint through uv run python -m tools. The RAM/log/clock ceilings in tools/godot.py are therefore load bearing rather than advisory: they exist only on that path, so a direct invocation is not a faster way to run a test, it is an unguarded one. This incident is the third power-cycle referenced by the never-reproduce-a-runaway rule.
recurrence: RECURRED 2026-10-03 after the guard was written. A second PC reset from the same memory-bloat class destroyed every live agent session: two of five build agents (character creation, world stage) lost work that was never committed and had to be redeployed from a written brief, while the quest/event/core slice survived only because a sibling agent had already committed it. The measured lesson is that the guard protects the machine but NOT the work: an uncommitted agent session is unrecoverable, so the binding constraint under a shared tree is commit frequency, not the RAM ceiling. Any orchestrator fanning out agents must treat 'is this slice committed' as part of its own state, because the agents that check their own git status after a reset are the ones that recover.

title: A probe was invoked by path instead of through tools test, so all three ceilings were absent and it reached 73 GB resident at 8.2 GB per 20s
impact: With 95 GB total the machine had roughly three minutes before an OOM would have destroyed every live agent's uncommitted work at once. Two processes were force-killed; RAM went from 19 GB free to 71 GB free. The disk side was never at risk (logs 0.00-0.02 MB).
cause: res://tests/_probe_ui_mem.gd was run directly rather than through uv run python -m tools test. tools/godot.py is what supplies --log-file redirection, the wall-clock ceiling and RAM_CEILING_BYTES. Invoked by path, every one of those guards is simply not in the process, so an allocating loop has no ceiling at all. The ceilings are not a property of the code; they are a property of the launcher.
guard: AGENTS.md now states the rule INC-0005 said was owed: tools/godot.py is the ONLY way to start the engine, because the RAM, log and clock ceilings live in that launcher and not in the code under test. Invoking the Godot binary by path gets no ceiling at all, so a silent allocating loop passes every guard that is not in the process. The rule also names the tempting failure mode directly - never reach for the binary to see the error the tool swallowed; read build/logs/ or raise a DEF/INC entry instead. The hazards themselves (unbounded wait, stranded mutation) remain unguarded because the hazard is in HOW Godot was started, not in what it ran.

title: Unscoped commits swept LIVE MUTATIONS into git history three times, where the working-tree guard cannot see them
impact: No work was lost - committed is recoverable - but HEAD briefly carried deliberately broken code, and a later git checkout or a fresh clone could have resurrected it. It also made the history misleading: one agent's commit contained only part of its own slice because the rest had been swept by another.
cause: INC-0003 is a bulk REVERT destroying work. This is the opposite and worse shape: a blanket stage or a bare git commit while a mutation was left applied in the working tree. Because a mutation is a deliberately broken line, committing it puts broken code INTO HISTORY, where it survives the restore that fixes the working tree. Three instances in one session: 9b26fc45 'commit all stale src codes' captured 3561 paths including an active mutation; a later commit captured 'var _actor: Actor = null # MUTANT_M1'; another captured 'if true: # MUT-M2'. The stranded-mutation guard scans res://src and res://tests in the WORKING TREE, so it reported clean while HEAD carried the marker.
guard: DUPLICATE OF INC-0007, recorded twice by the orchestrator in one turn - kept rather than deleted, per the never-delete rule, because the duplication is itself the trace. The live guard is INC-0007's: AGENTS.md rule 7 plus the git commit --only practice and an unfiltered git status --short, with the sequencing rule (never leave a mutation applied while other agents run) as the real enforcement, since test_no_stranded_mutation.gd reads the working tree and cannot see history.

title: An unscoped commit swept a LIVE MUTATION into git history three times, where the working-tree guard cannot see it
impact: No committed work was lost - committed is recoverable, and the marker was forward-fixed each time - but HEAD briefly carried deliberately broken code, which a later git checkout or a fresh clone could resurrect. It also split one agent's slice across two SHAs with a commit message that did not describe its work. The stranded-mutation guard reported clean throughout, because it scans the working tree and the working tree was already repaired.
cause: A blanket stage, or a bare git commit after a git add that swept paths another agent had already staged, while a MUTATION was left applied. Because a mutation is a deliberately broken line, committing it puts broken code into HISTORY, where it survives the working-tree restore that fixes the damage. Three instances: a 3561-path commit titled 'commit all stale src codes' captured an active mutation; another captured 'var _actor: Actor = null  # MUTANT_M1'; a third captured 'if true:  # MUT-M2'. A related shape: an agent's git add staged a concurrent agent's in-flight edits, and that agent's next commit published them - so the reverse case is a commit containing work its author did not write.
guard: AGENTS.md rule 7 requires staging only your own paths per vertical slice, which is the rule; the practice that actually closes it is git commit --only with explicit paths plus reading git status --short WITHOUT a pathspec filter, because a filtered view hides another agent's staged entries - two agents reported that filter hiding live staged work. INC-0003 covers the bulk REVERT; this is the opposite direction. Not tool-enforceable: the stranded-mutation guard reads the working tree, so the sequencing rule is the real guard - never leave a mutation applied while other agents run, and prefer mutating a throwaway copy the way tools cultivation mutate does.

title: An orchestrating agent reached for the Godot binary by path to isolate a bug, the exact INC-0004/INC-0005 shape
impact: No runaway was observed and no work was lost, but the attempted invocations had no RAM, log or clock ceiling in the process, so nothing would have stopped an allocating loop. Same mechanism that reached 73 GB in INC-0005 and forced the machine reset recorded as INC-0004. Caught only because the command was rejected and the sanctioned path was found in AGENTS.md.
cause: While debugging destiny I wrote a throwaway probe and tried to run it as a tools subcommand, then considered invoking the resolved Godot path directly. The stated intent was that it would be faster and would surface an error the tool had swallowed. Both are the INC-0005 mechanism: tools/godot.py supplies --log-file, the wall-clock ceiling and RAM_CEILING_BYTES, so starting the engine by path removes every guard. A run that produces no output passes all three ceilings by producing nothing measurable.
guard: Guarded by the AGENTS.md rule added for INC-0004: tools/godot.py is the only way to start the engine, and an unguarded invocation is not a faster way to run a test. The practice that stopped it here was to check the subcommand help before falling back to a path, and to prefer reading build/logs/ over reproducing. A probe that only needs to read module behaviour belongs in the test suite behind --suite, where the ceilings apply.

title: Orchestrator ran the Godot binary by path for every status-program diagnostic probe
impact: Six direct binary invocations during the status program, each with no RAM, log or clock ceiling in the process. No runaway observed and no work lost, but this is the exact INC-0004/INC-0005/INC-0008 mechanism that reached 73 GB and forced the machine reset recorded in INC-0004.
cause: To observe behaviour I wrote throwaway probes under game/src and ran them via the resolved Godot path instead of through uv run python -m tools test --suite. tools/godot.py is what supplies --log-file redirection, RAM_CEILING_BYTES and the wall-clock ceiling; a path invocation has none of them, so an allocating loop has no guard at all and a silent one passes every ceiling by producing nothing measurable.
guard: tools/godot_bypass.py (PREAMBLE_STEPS, 0.36s, engine-free) refuses any committed script that reads .godot-bin, resolves GODOT_BIN, or hands an engine flag to a godot executable, naming file, line and the ceilings it skips. Docs are exempt from the config-path rules but not from bare invocation, so naming the rule is allowed while shipping a runnable command is not. Verified RED on a planted .ps1 and clean on the tree. AGENTS.md still forbids the reach, and loop_guard covers the inline-shell case this cannot see.

title: git commit -- <paths> does not limit a commit to those paths
impact: A commit intended to add one test file also committed 15 files a concurrent agent had staged: tribulation, market and two ADR edits. No work was lost -- the staged content is byte-identical in the new commit and the agent's working tree is clean rather than staged -- but the commit is misattributed and the other agent's atomic unit is now welded to a test commit.
cause: git commit -- <pathspec> only asks git to do path-limited bookkeeping on the paths it names; it does NOT restrict the commit to them. It commits the WHOLE index, so every path another agent had already staged was swept in. The repo rule 'stage only your own paths' protects against `git add -A`; it is not sufficient on its own, because the index is shared too.
guard: AGENTS.md: before committing, `git diff --cached --name-only` must list ONLY paths you own. On a shared tree, also confirm nothing foreign is already staged at `git status --short` (a leading column means staged, not untracked). If foreign paths are staged, unstage them (`git restore --staged <path>`, path by path) or wait -- do not commit the index.

title: git commit --only swept 157 lines of an abandoned agent's uncommitted work into a 2-line fix
impact: The swept content was uncommitted and therefore unrecoverable, so committing it preserved rather than destroyed it, and nation stayed green at 720 passed / 0 failed. But the commit is titled as a two-token repair and its size does not match its message, so the history misdescribes what it contains. An agent that later reads it cannot tell which 157 lines were reviewed by anyone - they were not.
cause: git commit --only <path> commits the path's ENTIRE working-tree state, not a selected hunk. nation/api.gd belonged to an agent that had been idle for 62 minutes with two parse errors, so its uncommitted work was swept in with my edit. This is the same hazard family as INC-0003 (a bulk revert destroys work) and INC-0007 (an unscoped commit captures a mutation), but with a third trigger nobody had named: the pathspec was explicit and narrow, and it still swept everything. Scoping the path is necessary and NOT sufficient.
guard: Before committing to a path another agent owned, run git diff --stat -- <path> and compare the line count to the size of your own edit. A count far larger than the edit means the path carried someone else's uncommitted work; stop and decide deliberately whether to commit it, split it, or leave it. Narrow pathspecs prevent sweeping OTHER files, never other EDITS in the same file.

title: My own gate_reach census was blind to a producer shape and reported 4 shipped triggers as permanently dead
impact: tools/gate_reach check reported 14 unbacked_demand gates, 4 of which had a live producer: app/world_ambient.gd:60 ROSTER supplied storm_front_sighted, void_seam_sounded, tournament_called and sect_war_called, dispatched through WorldAmbient.due -> app/world_pulse.gd:332 -> offer() -> app/beat_director.gd:122 WorldFact.record. Four event triggers were called dead while the world was in fact saying them. The census documented two producer shapes (a member expression, and a scalar StringName const) and this was a third: a static roster reached through a class in a DIFFERENT file, four hops from the writer. A false red is worse here than a false green, because it sends an agent to author a producer that already exists - the exact ADR 0066 quiet lie, produced by a gate rather than by prose.
cause: code_owned_supply scanned ONE file at a time and resolved ids only from a literal at the writer call or from a const in the SAME file. world_pulse.gd holds const AMBIENT_FACTS := WorldAmbient.ROSTER - a reference to a table, carrying no ids at all - so even a same-file roster reader would have read zero. The gate had a documented blind spot (its own item 1, 'a producer assembled at run time') and I read it as covering this, when it covered only run-time assembly, not a cross-file static table. I wrote the blind-spot list and then did not test the list against a producer that actually existed.
guard: Two gates, and the mutation that proves them. (1) Teach the roster: _ROSTER_OPEN/_ROSTER_FACT read a static fact table, and _roster_files resolves it through class_name so the table is read from the file that DECLARES it, never from the caller's reference to it. (2) The roster counts ONLY when a class whose file both declares a roster and dispatches it is named in a static call by a file that reaches the writer - _ROSTER_DISPATCH plus _static_class_calls. MUTATION-A removed that dispatch guard and unbacked fell 10 -> 3, i.e. it counted 8 fact ids nothing produces, which is the false-green the guard exists to prevent; restored, 10 again. General rule for any future producer shape: when a gate reports a gate dead, check for a live producer BEFORE authoring one, and add the new shape to the census in the SAME change - which the module's own header already demanded and I had not been doing.

title: The stranded-mutation guard reads the working tree only, so a probe committed into history is invisible to it and fails open forever
impact: test_no_stranded_mutation.gd reads res://src and res://tests off disk and matches five marker shapes rooted at MUTATION. A probe that reaches a COMMIT is therefore permanently undetectable by the one guard meant to catch it: the checkout is clean, the marker is in history, and every future run passes. A probe that returned a wrong value and was then committed ships as the implementation, and no suite in this repo can tell. This is INC-0007 generalised: that one was a specific double-dispatch that captured another agent's MUTANT-B1, which was forward-fixed by hand; nothing structural prevents the next one, and CI runs exactly tools check, so it would pass.
cause: The guard was written to stop an agent leaving a probe in the tree at the end of a session, which is a working-tree hazard by nature. It was never given a history check, and git history is not reachable from GDScript at test time. Measured 2026-10-03: git log --all -S MUTATION-W2 over game/src returns nothing, so the specific incident an agent reported had in fact been cleaned before I looked - but the blind spot is structural, not dependent on that probe having existed.
guard: Shipped: tools/mutation_history.py + tools/mutation_history_cmd.py, wired into tools check as 'mutation_history check'. Git is unreachable from GDScript at test time, so the working-tree half stays in test_no_stranded_mutation.gd and the history half lives in Python. Three bugs found by mutation, all of which had made the tool report CLEAN on a repo containing a committed probe: (1) _first_guarded_path read the file from disk instead of the blob, so a probe introduced and later reverted read as clean - exactly the class the tool exists to find; (2) the regex SHAPES were passed to 'git log -S', which is a substring count and not a regex, so every pickaxe matched nothing; (3) fixed-whitespace literals like '# MUTATION' would miss a tab or double space, so the pickaxe now searches the ROOTS (MARKER, 'XXX MUTAT') and the regexes decide, reading each blob. Proven with a probe committed to a throwaway worktree (never the shared branch): the sweep failed naming the commit, and after removing the worktree it reports only the two real ones. Prose control: 4 legitimate mutation-prose cases pass, all 5 marker shapes flag. It found 2 REAL committed probes on first run - 5f0dee4fc3e7 (game/tests/modules/loot/loot_screen_rig.gd:196 MUTATION-PROBE-A) and f9d8ab5d2322 (game/src/modules/mind_cultivation/breakthrough_condition.gd MUTATION-BL0161) - so the hazard had already occurred twice and INC-0007 was not the only instance.

title: A broad commit titled 'commit items' swept a half-finished sect/nation refactor onto main and broke every agent's verification
impact: No committed work was lost, but main stopped compiling: SectReadModel could not be resolved, NationApi.act did not exist yet and app/institution_resolver.gd still called the not-yet-moved act(). A parse error aborts suite loads process-wide, so every agent's run went red for reasons outside their own slice - measured here as ~52 event assertions failing with reason 'no_actor' that reduced to two parse errors in files this agent did not own.
cause: Commit f9d8ab5d is titled 'commit items' and carries 108 paths: an entire sect/nation act/schism/read-model refactor, plus app/actor_factory.gd and two files belonging to the narrative program (core/world_fact.gd, app/character_creation_flow.gd). The refactor was incomplete at the moment of the sweep, so the commit captured a slice mid-refactor rather than at a compiling boundary. Distinct from INC-0007 and INC-0011 in the trigger: no mutation marker and no narrow pathspec - the hazard is an INCOMPLETE REFACTOR staged alongside unrelated work, so no scope check catches it.
guard: A commit must land on a COMPILING tree; a mid-refactor commit is the same hazard as a stranded mutation because both put a knowingly-unbuildable state into history. The check is the one every agent already runs: uv run python -m tools arch plus the targeted --suite run BEFORE committing, which is what would have refused this commit. Second half, and the part that cost the most time here: when a suite fails with 'no_actor' or a compile error in a module you do not own, ATTRIBUTE it before changing your own code. 52 event failures reduced to two parse errors in another agent's files, and the correct action was to leave them alone and verify only the slices that do not depend on them.

title: A shortened map theme desynced 260 index rows from the generator with every gate green, because nothing compared the two sides
impact: tools/map_assets.py:363 writes environment_theme into every row of game/assets/map-asset-index.jsonl from ENVIRONMENT_THEMES, and that prose is pasted verbatim into ComfyUI prompts, so it is the text that renders an image rather than a label. Commit 7bf3e4bc shortened four of those strings to fit a line budget. The generator was never re-run and migrate cannot refresh an existing value, so 260 rows across 4 themes kept prose the source no longer contained and every gate in the repo stayed green: no check compared the index against the generator. The result renders as visibly wrong art with a green build, and the cause is invisible to review because the diff is four strings that read as fine. 373ffd06 fixed it by value-preserving implicit concatenation, which is also the reason tools fmt must never be allowed to re-wrap that text: ruff format joins implicitly-concatenated literals that fit on one line, so a wrap that fixes lint and gets reverted is not a fix.
cause: The check did not exist. There was a guard for every other number-shaped table in this repo - realm_power check, technique_power check, difficulty check, gate_reach - and none for the map asset index, on the reasoning that generated data cannot drift from its generator. That reasoning is false in one direction: the generator is edited by hand and the data is not, and the one migration that would reconcile them explicitly cannot update an existing value. I had already measured the drift with a throwaway probe in build/ and filed it as a NEXT step rather than shipping it, which is the same deferral that left map_assets.py idle for 90 minutes and then committed (BL-0401).
guard: Shipped: tools/map_theme.py, wired into tools check as 'map_theme check'. Every environment_theme in game/assets/map-asset-index.jsonl must appear among the VALUES of ENVIRONMENT_THEMES - the index stores the prose, not the environment key, and comparing against the keys reports all 19 themes missing, which is the one mistake available here. Deliberately one-directional: a source theme with no index row is an unused theme, a content choice, not a defect, and failing on it would cry wolf on the next theme authored before its art. A vacuity check refuses to pass when the index names no theme at all. Mutation-proven both ways: replacing one exported value turns the check red naming 19 themes over 1245 rows, and restoring it returns 19-of-19 over 1235 rows. Guard the concatenation explicitly in any future edit - the prose must stay an implicitly-concatenated literal.

title: Every guard in tools/ shipped with no test of its own, so a loosened validator reported ok while the tree was broken
impact: Not a runaway and not disk: a coverage hole with a specific blast radius. All validators in this repo are Python modules run by tools check, and the GDScript suite cannot reach any of them, so a guard shipped in tools/ had no test asserting it still fails. The failure mode is the worst kind for a validator - a guard quietly loosened keeps printing ok while the thing it watches is broken. Not hypothetical: gate_reach was blind to the roster producer shape long enough to report four shipped event triggers as permanently dead (INC-0012), and mutation_history shipped with three bugs in a row that each made it report clean on a repo containing a committed probe (INC-0013). Both printed ok.
cause: The architecture assumed guards are covered by being run in check, which is true of a guard PASS path and false of its FAIL path. Nothing asserted that gate_reach goes red on a roster nothing dispatches, or that map_theme rejects a theme with no prose, or that mutation_history finds a probe. tools/ has no test harness at all - no pytest, no test_*.py under tools/ - so there was nowhere to put such an assertion. The tell was visible: map_theme and mutation_history both shipped with prose arguing how they must not be loosened, and no mechanism held them to their own argument.
guard: Shipped: tools/selftest.py (harness) and tools/selftest_cases.py (cases), wired into tools check as selftest run before the other content audits since it needs no engine. Every case asserts a RED path against a temp fixture; none edits the repository. Two narrow seams added so guards can be exercised off the real tree: mutation_history.REPO and map_theme.authored_prose/unbacked. Four mutations run, three caught (the gate_reach roster dispatch guard, the mutation_history pickaxe, map_theme values() vs keys()). The fourth - mutating the harness own except clause - is NOT caught and is recorded rather than hidden: a harness has no test of its test. A green selftest means the guards still go red, not that the harness is correct.

title: My mutation_history guard asked whether a probe was EVER committed, which is permanently true once true, so tools check could never pass again
impact: A design flaw in the guard I shipped as INC-0013 mitigation. sweep() walked git log --all -S and reported every commit that ever carried a marker. History is immutable, so that question has a permanently-yes answer after the first incident: the repo had two such commits, so mutation_history check would have failed on EVERY run from then on. A gate that cannot go green is worth less than no gate, because the first agent to see it red and unfixable will downgrade it or delete it, and both destroy the protection. I did not notice for hours because my own new self-test asserted the sweep FINDS a probe - which it did, correctly, on a fixture dirty by construction. The test confirmed the mechanism and never asked whether the gate was satisfiable.
cause: The guard conflated two questions: has a probe ever been committed (a historical fact, immutable) versus does a shipped ref tip carry a probe (current state, repairable). Only the second is gateable. I built the check around the evidence - two probes genuinely were committed - rather than around what the check is for. Nothing in tools check asks whether a stage is satisfiable, and I never asked, because every stage I had run returned ok until it did not.
guard: Redesigned to gate on ref TIPS: carried() runs one git grep per shipped ref tip (refs/heads/, refs/remotes/, plus a detached HEAD) filtered through SHAPE_RE, so a repaired probe goes green while a live one still fails. Agent-local namespaces (refs/stash, refs/recovery/, refs/codex/) are skipped as machine-local invisible state rather than the repository. The self-test pins BOTH directions - a tip carrying a probe is found, and a repaired tip is clean - and the second case is the one that stops the guard becoming unsatisfiable again. Standing lesson for any validator added to tools check: a guard must be able to return ok on a repaired tree. Prove that once, in the self-test, BEFORE shipping the guard.

title: Concurrent agents saturate the single Godot project lock, so test runs starve with no gap to acquire it
impact: Measured 2026-10-04. tools/godot.py serialises every Godot invocation behind one OS-level advisory lock (msvcrt.locking on build/logs/godot.lock), LOCK_WAIT_SECONDS = 900. With the fleet this repo now runs, that lock was held continuously for over 40 minutes: I polled a 200s window at 10s intervals and never saw it free, and the holder was a DIFFERENT run each time (pids 71564/54736 at 02:42, fresh processes with an actively written log). The failure is starvation, not a hang. An agent whose wait expires raises another Godot run has held godot.lock for more than 900s, which reads as a broken gate rather than as contention - and the natural reaction is to delete the lock. That would be the BL-0424 mistake on a lock with a live owner: two headless runs over game/.godot is a corruption shape, not a slow one.
cause: The lock is correct and necessary - it stops concurrent runs interleaving writes to the shared import cache and editor state. The defect is that LOCK_WAIT_SECONDS treats contention and a crashed owner identically: both surface as held too long, so there is no way to tell a live queue from a dead holder, and the only safe response to an ambiguous lock is to wait. Nothing publishes the holder pid or how long it has held. I very nearly deleted it myself - the file was 22 hours old and empty, which looks exactly like a stale lock, and it was not: an OS advisory lock ignores mtime entirely.
guard: tools/godot.py writes build/logs/godot.lock.owner ({pid, since}) once the lock is acquired and clears it before release. On wait expiry the message now names the holder and its age and says WAIT; with no sidecar it says so plainly and says re-run, correct under either kernel answer because the lock is mutual exclusion rather than a flag. It never says delete the file. _clear_lock_owner removes only its own pid, so a dead owner sidecar survives as evidence. Three red-path selftest cases. Not exercised under real contention, and whether msvcrt drops the lock on process death is asserted nowhere.

title: Unbounded loops reached main through sub-agents that were never told about them
impact: The two disk/RAM blasts were fixed at the site, but nothing stopped the next one arriving the same way
cause: Loop-awareness lived as prose in AGENTS.md and in my own head. A sub-agent dispatched with a feature brief inherits nothing about it, so an unguarded while shipped into res://src or res://tests and I inherited it. There was also no instruction to FIX a loop found incidentally.
guard: AGENTS.md workflow step 3: every dispatched agent must be loop-aware before it writes a loop and name the guard before reporting done; a loop found is fixed in the same change; search the shape with rg; the fix carries one lean comment naming hazard and guard. test_no_unbounded_wait.gd is the build backstop.

title: A concurrent agent removed DestinyProjection.events() without repointing its three callers, and nothing compiled
impact: Every suite in the repo failed to load, including four that were green minutes earlier and have no dependency on destiny. Verified by grep: the sole cause of 7 soul_death_loop failures was that parse error.
cause: destiny_projection.gd lost `static func events()` while destiny/api.gd still calls it at lines 175, 225 and 385. A parse error in a facade that every module imports takes the WHOLE suite down, which is the DEF-0143 shape applied to a removed method rather than a corrupted file.
guard: tools boot runs BEFORE tools test in tools/check.py, so a facade that cannot compile surfaces in seconds rather than after the suite -- the ordering already existed and did its job. Verified resolved: DestinyProjection.events() is declared (destiny_projection.gd:204) and all three api.gd callers resolve; modules/destiny reports 1217 passed with zero parse errors and zero load failures. The repo-wide parse-error count is now zero, after defining the missing at_channel_cap that body_cultivation/training.gd:146 called (b85f2c62). title: An inline python -c image writer looped forever on an unreachable stdin sentinel
impact: 11.6 GB resident / 42.8 GB commit at 9067 s CPU in one python process, outside every ceiling; killed by hand
cause: A sub-agent composed a one-liner reading base64 from stdin: iter(lambda: sys.stdin.readline().strip().encode(), b'END_IMAGE_DATA'). At EOF readline returns '', and ''.strip().encode() is b', which can NEVER equal the b'END_IMAGE_DATA' sentinel, so the stop condition is unreachable and b''.join() appended forever. Non-terminating loop plus unbounded allocation, with no log output to trip any ceiling.
guard: tools/loop_guard.py refuses a command whose iter(callable, sentinel) cannot be satisfied, because .strip().encode() maps EOF to b' and never to a marker; it also refuses an unbounded stdin while-True. Three selftest red-path cases (INC-0021 verbatim, a reachable sentinel, a terminating generator) keep it honest. AGENTS.md workflow step 3 requires running it before any inline python -c that reads stdin or loops.

title: The unbounded-wait arch guard reports a false positive on a provably bounded find() loop
impact: test_no_unbounded_wait is red on a clean tree, so the guard that is supposed to catch real runaways is instead crying wolf on a loop that terminates in at most len(s)/len(needle) passes
cause: The guard accepts a while only if it moves a counter it reads, drains the container it tests, fills toward a fixed count, or breaks/returns. `while at != -1: at = calls.find(needle, at + needle.length())` in tests/app/test_screen_reachability.gd does none of those by name: it advances a SEARCH INDEX through a String, which is the same shape as a counter but is not one the rule can see. It is genuinely bounded -- every pass advances at by at least needle.length(), so iterations <= len(calls)/len(needle), verified over seven inputs and a dense 5000-char worst case.
guard: Accept path 6 in test_no_unbounded_wait.gd: a while whose body reassigns the tested index via x = s.find(needle, x + needle.length()) -- a search index advanced strictly past its own match. Narrow by construction: find(needle, at) stands still and find(needle, at - 1) walks backwards, so neither can match, and INC-0001 s own never-true state shape is pinned as still rejected. Scoped to the loop body by its own while line, so a find() in a different function cannot be read as this loop advancing. Pinned by test_search_index_rule_shape.gd: 13 cases, 7 of them the reject side, on fixtures rather than the tree. The shipped loop was NOT edited to make the guard pass.

title: A mutation reached the git INDEX while two agents shared one file, and no guard sees that layer
impact: Near miss, caught by reading the index before committing. No commit landed and no marker entered history, so the cost was one reset of one file. What WOULD have cost: a shipped MUTATION marker in history, which test_no_stranded_mutation.gd cannot catch (INC-0007 - a working-tree guard cannot see the index or a commit).
cause: Mutation testing makes a file WRONG ON PURPOSE, then reverts it. The window between apply and revert is a period in which the file is not the code anyone intends. Three things had to coincide and none of them is checked: (1) agent A applies a mutation to game/src/modules/loot/loot_state.gd for mutation testing; (2) agent B, recovering from its own error, runs git add on that same file - staging whatever the working tree currently holds, mutation included; (3) some third agent commits. INC-0011 tells an agent to run git diff --stat before committing, which catches FOREIGN EDITS IN A FILE it is committing. It does not tell an agent to check whether a staged file contains a live mutation marker, because git diff --cached is a different command from git diff and neither is in the shared-tree rules.
guard: mutation_history.staged() reads the INDEX with git grep --cached, so the answer depends on the staged blobs and not on the working tree -- the incident had a CORRECT file on disk and the probe in the index, so every worktree reader saw nothing. conflicted() additionally reads the stage-1/2/3 entries an unmerged path has instead of a stage-0 one, which git grep cannot see, and readable() refuses to read an unreadable index as clean. carried() calls staged() first, so a staged probe fails tools check before it is ever committed; mutation_history check is in PREAMBLE_STEPS. Verified against a temp repo by redirecting REPO: clean index reports 0, a probe staged with a repaired worktree reports 1, restaging the repair clears it. 16 mutation selftest cases pin both sides.

title: An agent staged a path while a mutation marker was live in it; the working-tree guard cannot see that
impact: Near miss only: the marker never reached a commit. Caught by reading git diff --cached after a file I had edited showed MM instead of M. Cost was one staged reset. Had it landed, the mutation marker would be permanent in history and unrecoverable by the working-tree guard.
cause: Two independent, individually-correct practices overlapped in time: (a) a mutation window, where I left MUTATION-LOOTWORLDFULL applied to game/src/modules/loot/loot_state.gd while proving a refusal-reason fix load-bearing, and (b) a peer agent running git add on that same file while recovering from an upstream error. The index then held a state that existed in neither HEAD nor the worktree. test_no_stranded_mutation.gd reads the WORKING TREE, so it is blind to a marker that lives only in the index, and equally blind to one already committed - the INC-0007 shape with a second entrance.
guard: mutation_history.staged() (tools/mutation_history.py:289) reads the INDEX with 'git grep --cached' and classifies through the SAME _live_marker helper the ref half uses, so the two layers cannot disagree about what a probe is; carried() surfaces index findings FIRST so a truncated report cannot drop the ones about to become history. Wired into tools check via carried(), which already gated ref findings. ADR 0156 records the decision and the fix-forward-revert trap that reading the worktree harder cannot close. Three red-path cases in tools/selftest_cases.py:626/660/694 assert (a) a staged probe is found while the probe is ABSENT from the worktree and the file reads MM, (b) restaging the repair clears the index AND carried() AND leaves no ref finding - a guard that can never pass gets deleted on its first trip, (c) the finding reaches carried(), which is what check gates. The GDScript tree guard (test_no_stranded_mutation.gd) is unchanged and still worktree-only: this closes the index layer, not the whole class.

title: A mutation proof can be silently invalidated because something else edits the mutated file mid-window, and the run then measures the CLEAN tree and reports GREEN
impact: Two mutation attempts on game/src/modules/mind_cultivation/training.gd were defeated. The first: the file hashed 7662AF23 with a MUTATION-B1 early return, and two minutes later hashed 94E882DA with the mutation gone, so the tripwire run reported 67 passed / 0 failed and would have been reported as 'the rewritten tripwire is blind' when it had in fact measured the restored tree. The second: the file came back as 7DDF7D16, a hash nobody authored, with the mutation INVERTED (if amount > 0.0: return became if amount <= 0.0: return) - a correct no-op guard, but not a mutation. Cost two full lock cycles and nearly produced a false negative claim about a test.
cause: A mutation window is only safe while the mutated bytes stay put, and this working tree is shared with live agents plus at least one process that rewrites files in it. The proof's failure mode is asymmetric and invisible: a mutation that gets repaired does not fail loudly, it produces a PASSING run, and 'the test passed' is indistinguishable from 'the tree was restored before the test read it'. Nothing in tools/godot.py records the source state a run measured.
guard: Record the mutated file's SHA256 in the run's own log BEFORE launching, and read it back after, so every run states what tree it measured - the third attempt embedded the hash in the attempt header and that is what made attribution possible. Prefer a mutation that reads as plausible (AWARENESS_RATE := 0.0) over one carrying a MUTATION- marker, because the marker is what an automated repair looks for. And treat 'the mutated suite went green' as an unmeasured run, never as evidence the guard is weak.

title: A bare 'git commit' committed a peer's staged index: 'git add <my path>' is necessary but NOT sufficient
impact: Commit a795c9c5 was titled and described as a one-file change to tools/godot.py and actually carried 14 files, 13 of them a peer's unrelated in-flight work (app/soul_death.gd +144, app/character_creation_program.gd +58, tests/modules/soul/* +421, modules/anchor/api.gd, tests/modules/save/test_save_envelope.gd, data/items/consumable/guardian_vigil_ash.tres, docs/incidents.jsonl and more). Nothing was lost - their work became durable, which is safer than leaving it uncommitted - but the commit message misdescribes its contents and a reader auditing that hash for the hermetic-run fix finds thirteen unrelated files. One of those files also carried a peer's LIVE mutation marker (MUTATION-EL-RESTORE-MOUNT on ElementsApi.apply_realm_modifiers in item_workbench_app.gd); my commit happened to remove it, which is the right direction, but it was luck rather than a guard.
cause: INC-0011 already says a narrow pathspec is necessary but not sufficient, and this is the missing half of that rule. I ran 'git add tools/godot.py' then a bare 'git commit -m'. The pathspec restricted what I STAGED; it did not restrict what was COMMITTED, because a bare commit serialises the entire index. With ~20 concurrent agents, the index is shared: a peer who ran 'git add' on their own files put them there, and my commit picked them up. The dangerous inverse also holds - a bare commit can commit a peer's half-finished mutation, which is what INC-0007 warns about. Nothing in the tooling detects this, because the commit succeeds and every file in it is a legitimate change by someone.
guard: git commit --only <path> for every commit in this tree, which restricts the COMMIT as well as the stage, so a shared index can never leak in. The check that would have caught it: after committing, 'git show --stat HEAD' must list only the paths the commit message describes - one command, and it is the step I skipped. Treat a commit whose stat lists a file you did not edit as a signal to amend the MESSAGE (never the content, which would destroy the peer's work) and to say so in the reply. No automated guard is proposed: a pre-commit hook cannot know which staged paths are mine, and the authors of the other thirteen are not recorded anywhere git keeps.

title: I committed another agents in-flight nation refactor, the exact INC-0011 mistake
impact: dead2780 carried 105 insertions and 155 deletions of another agents uncommitted work alongside my 14-line repoint; the rest of that refactor (nation_resolve.gd and three sibling files) is still uncommitted, so the commit is a partial slice of someones feature
cause: I ran git diff --stat, saw 260 lines changed against my 14-line edit, and committed anyway because the file was the one I was fixing. Staging only my paths was not enough: git commit --only commits a paths ENTIRE working-tree state, which is the half of the rule I knew and the half I did not apply to a file I had edited myself.
guard: PENDING. What dead2780 actually did: it carried the other agents verdict_view refactor in api.gd (105 insertions, 155 deletions) alongside my 14-line repoint. title: I dispatched an agent into a lane another session already held, by reading the claim rule and not using the claim tool
impact: Two live sessions were one edit away from a write-write collision in game/src/modules/loot/**, game/tests/modules/loot/** and game/data/loot/**, over the same backlog id BL-0136. No work was lost: the peer had not committed and my agent had not written, so standing the duplicate down cost one message. That was luck rather than a control - if the peer had committed first, or my agent had opened the same file, neither agent could have told which lines were whose.
cause:
I dispatched a background subagent to own BL-0136 (stranded boss drops) in game/src/modules/loot/**, game/tests/modules/loot/** and game/data/loot/**, having just read the new AGENTS.md rule that says to claim paths BEFORE dispatching (INC-0023) - and having not done it. The claim_guard ledger existed and was green; I simply did not consult it. Minutes later a check of the working tree showed 64 dirty files in exactly that lane, including loot_validator.gd (+61) and loot_content.gd (+146) whose diff already names BL-0136 in its own comments, plus a new untracked test_loot_payable_tables.gd. Another session was mid-implementation of the same backlog id in the same files. Two sessions about to edit the same paths is the write-write collision INC-0023 exists to prevent, and I had the tool that would have told me not to.
The failure is a sequence, not a moment. I read the new rule, deployed two agents, and only ran claim_guard report AFTER a Godot lock had queued for minutes - i.e. the check happened while I was blocked on something else, so it cost nothing to skip. The dispatch itself is the irreversible step: once a session is live it is already writing. Claiming afterwards is not a mitigation, it is a note in a ledger describing a collision that may already have lost work.
What made it recoverable this time is that the peer had not committed and I had not written yet, so standing the duplicate down cost a message rather than a merge. That is luck, not a control: had the peer committed first, or had my agent opened the same file, the damage would have been two agents editing one function with neither able to tell which lines were theirs.
Guard: run claim_guard claim with the session id BEFORE the dispatch call, never after, and treat a dispatch into a path nobody has claimed as a decision you must be able to justify rather than a free choice. The cheap discipline is to make the claim part of the same breath as the dispatch - claim, then dispatch, and if the claim fails pick a different lane rather than proceeding. claim_guard check already fails on overlap and runs in tools check, so a collision is visible to everyone within one gate run; the gap was purely that I did not look before acting.
Also worth stating: my first instinct on discovering the collision was to re-brief the agent, which would have doubled down on it. Standing a duplicate down is the correct move and it needs no permission, because the duplicate is me by construction.
guard:
PARTLY WRONG, AND THE WRONG PART IS THE IMPACT AND CAUSE. Read the guard; distrust the story of a collision.

WHAT STANDS. I dispatched a background agent to own BL-0136 in modules/loot without claiming the paths first, which AGENTS.md forbids (INC-0023). Claiming before dispatch is correct and remains the guard.

WHAT DOES NOT STAND. This entry previously said a peer was mid-implementation of the same backlog id in the same files and that two live sessions were one edit from a write-write collision. That did not happen. I saw 64 dirty files in the lane, assumed a peer, and stood the agent down. The agent then reported those files were ITS OWN edits - loot_content.gd +146, loot_validator.gd +61, both matching the counts I had cited as evidence of a peer. So there was one session, not two, and the collision described here is one I manufactured by reading my own agent's work as somebody else's.

THE REAL COST, and it is worse than a near-miss. Because I stopped the agent mid-slice its work is now unverified: it reported never executing its code, and its own suite reds 4 cases whose output contradicts an independent scan I ran (8 unpayable tables against my 0, where the nested closure from 336 bound tables reaches all 1425 authored ones). One suite in the shared tree is red because of work nobody adopted and nobody reviewed. That is worse than the collision I avoided, and it came from the same error - deciding what the evidence meant before establishing who produced it.

THE LESSON. A dirty file in a lane I dispatched into is not evidence of a peer; it is the expected state of a lane I dispatched into, because that is what the agent was told to do. Before attributing work to a peer, ask whether it is my own agent's, and check a claim before acting on either story. Standing a duplicate session down is still correct and still needs no permission, but only after establishing there IS a duplicate.

The sub-agent's own report is what corrected this, which is the argument for requiring agents to state what they wrote: it listed exact paths and line counts matching what I had misattributed. An agent that names its own writes is checkable; one that reports only conclusions is not.

title: A peer commit with a very long asset path can fail every other session's commit with 'Filename too long'
impact: One commit attempt in this session failed with 'Filename too long' after a character wave added game/assets/characters/unique-index-wave-10.jsonl. My own staged work - a probe fix and two backlog entries - was blocked by a path I neither created nor own, and the failure is silent about the cause: git names the offending file rather than saying which of MY paths triggered it, so the message reads as if my commit were malformed. It also did not corrupt the index and did not lose the staged work, so the cost was a retry rather than data.
cause: Windows MAX_PATH. A repository holding deep asset paths accumulates them without bound, and git will not commit a tree containing a path it cannot represent unless core.longpaths is enabled. Nobody here decided to raise the limit, so the limit simply arrived, and it arrives as a global side effect: one session's asset choice blocks every other session's commit, which is the opposite of how the shared-tree rules are meant to distribute risk.
guard: Treat a 'Filename too long' commit failure as a tree problem, not a message problem: retry with the message in a FILE (git commit -F) to rule out shell quoting, and if it still fails, the path belongs to whoever added it. Do not go looking for a shorter name for your own paths - your paths were fine. Raising core.longpaths is the real fix and it is a repository-level decision that belongs to whoever owns the asset pipeline, not to a session that happened to trip it. The recovery is cheap and worth stating: staged work survives the failure, so re-run the same commit once the tree is fixed rather than redoing the work.

title: I committed a peers loot work a SECOND time, defeating a guard I had just written
impact: d34cb083 carries 136 lines of a peers uncommitted work (AFFLICTION_FIELD, unbanded_tables, band_bound_tables, band_reachable_item_ids, bound_table_ids) under my commit message. Nothing was lost and nothing is broken, but their slice is now attributed to me and they may not realise their work is committed.
cause: I knew the hazard -- I wrote the rule for it earlier this session (INC-0011, INC-0029) -- and still walked into it. I staged only my18-line hunk with update-index --cacheinfo, verified git diff --cached was exactly 18 insertions, and then ran git commit --only, which OVERRIDES the index and takes the paths ENTIRE working-tree state. So the careful staging was discarded by the very command meant to use it. The guard I wrote checks the staged diff; the commit path I chose never reads it.
guard: AGENTS.md workflow rule 7 now states the two are INCOMPATIBLE rather than implying pathspec scoping suffices: git commit --only reads the WORKING TREE and ignores a hand-built index, so commit exactly what you staged with NO pathspec, or commit a whole path with --only when that path is dirty with your work alone, never both. The deciding number is git diff --cached --ignore-cr-at-eol --stat, because a CRLF-only rewrite reads as hundreds of changed lines and hides a small real hunk. Second occurrence after INC-0029, which is why the wording changed from a check to a choice. NOT mechanised: nothing in tools/ enforces it, so this is prose and can be repeated.

title: A subagent dispatch returned no sessionID at all, leaving the outcome ambiguous and the paths claimed with no session to attribute
impact: Dispatching an agent for BL-0110 into modules/items returned a tool result carrying no sessionID - not a failure message, an absent body. There is then no way to tell whether the session started and is working, or never started at all, which is exactly the ambiguity AGENTS.md now names. The paths were already claimed as root-bl0110 from my own dispatch, so the claim ledger shows a live owner that no session corresponds to, and the claim will keep looking healthy to claim_guard check for hours. The claim was made by me and is not stale by the ledger's own definition, so nothing will clear it.
cause: A dispatch whose result body is empty has two indistinguishable causes: the session started and the transport lost the id, or the session never started. Nothing in the ledger distinguishes them, because the ledger records path ownership and not dispatch outcomes. The risk is asymmetric in the direction of re-sending: if the session did start, re-sending the identical prompt puts two of my own sessions on one path, which is the write-write collision INC-0023 exists to prevent, and the duplicate is invisible precisely because claim_guard would see one claim covering both. If it did not start, re-sending costs nothing but a second id. So the safe reading is the pessimistic one, and it leaves the work undone rather than doubled.
guard: HALF MECHANISED, and the mechanism is the half that could be. (1) The orphaned claim root-bl0110 is RELEASED, after sampling its paths twice over ~2 minutes: zero files changed, its one dirty file last written 7 min prior, and12 live git processes working elsewhere. Consistent with no session, not proof. (2) tools/claim_guard.py grows an `orphaned` field, set by claim --orphaned, REPORTED by check on every run and never fatal (the staleness shape, for the INC-0017 reason: a claim must not be failed for confessing). Silent was the defect -- an orphaned claim is indistinguishable from a healthy one to every reader. Two bugs my own checks caught while building it: write_claims hardcoded three fields so the flag was parsed, reported and silently dropped on write; and bool(false) is True, so a non-boolean orphaned flipped healthy claims. Still PROSE: whether the dispatch started is unanswerable from the tree, so reading the sessionID out of the previous tool result before re-sending remains a rule no tool can enforce.

title: probe: concurrent write made tools CLI unreadable
impact: one wrong diagnosis
cause: half-written module read mid-write
guard: FIRST, A CORRECTION TO THIS ENTRY''S OWN TITLE, WHICH SAYS "probe" AND SHOULD NOT: this is not a probe, it is an incident. The tools incident interface has add (title, impact, cause, guard, status) and close (guard, status only) and NO update action, so a title can only be set at creation - the terse title, the one-line impact and the one-line cause above are what the first add managed to record, and the full record lives here because `close --guard` is the only field `close` will write. An agent reading this entry should read THIS field, not the title. THE HAZARD: a concurrent agent''s non-atomic write made the shared tools CLI transiently unreadable, and the traceback named a file the reader never touched. IMPACT: one wrong diagnosis and one wasted diagnostic round. `uv run python -m tools new_adr --help` returned a traceback ending `NameError: name PREmise_state is not defined. Did you mean: PREMISE_STATE?` at tools/cultivation/mutate.py:222, which reads as the ENTIRE tools entrypoint being broken, because tools/__main__.py imports selftest_cases -> cultivation.selftest_case -> cultivation.mutate at startup, so one unreadable file takes down every task. No repo change was broken and nothing was lost; the same command worked minutes earlier and again immediately after, and backlog/deferred/incident validate and cultivation validate all ran clean throughout. CAUSE: observed ONCE, and the mechanism is inference from the traceback rather than a second observation. A NameError for a name plainly declared elsewhere in the same file is the signature of Python evaluating a HALF-WRITTEN module - the importing process opened tools/cultivation/mutate.py while another session was mid-write, which is consistent with git status showing that file as ` M` at the time. Nothing in the failure names the writer, so the reader''s only evidence is that the identifier differs from the suggestion by case alone, and the cheap wrong conclusion is that the repo is broken rather than that a file is being rewritten under them. This is the Python-side analogue of DEF-0143 (a transient core script corruption silently breaking every test run), and worse in one respect: there the error was invisible, here it is loud and confidently wrong. GUARD, prose and not mechanised, honestly so: (1) re-run the command once before concluding anything is broken - the window is milliseconds and the retry is free, and a NameError whose Did-you-mean suggestion is the same identifier with different case is a half-written-file signature, not a code defect. (2) Before diagnosing a tooling failure, run `git status` on the path the traceback NAMES: if it is ` M` or untracked and you do not own it, another session is mid-write and the failure is theirs. (3) The eager selftest_cases import in tools/__main__.py is why a transient write is repo-wide rather than task-local; a lazy import would bound the blast radius to the one task. Not mechanised because there is no shared lock on the Python sources and no import-error classifier, so this stays a rule an agent has to know. STATUS is `watching`, not `mitigated`: nothing bounds this, and saying `mitigated` would claim a ceiling that does not exist.

title: THIRD occurrence in two turns: 'git add <path>' then a bare 'git commit' serialises the shared index. The habit is the defect, not the slip
impact: Commit 45cfc2e5-adjacent work shipped 18 asset files (15 insertions, 218 deletions, including binary PNGs and .import files) alongside a two-entry backlog edit, because I staged one path and then committed with no pathspec. Nothing was lost - the assets were already staged by their author and are now durable in HEAD - but the hash is titled for a backlog reconciliation and carries an asset deletion wave. This is the same shape as two earlier incidents today: INC-0028 (14 files) and the amend that dropped fertility/api.gd. Three occurrences makes this a behavioural pattern rather than a slip, and a rule that has been restated twice and not followed is not a rule.
cause: The two forms are mutually exclusive and I keep alternating between them. git add <path> plus a BARE git commit commits the whole index, which in a shared tree holds every peer's staged work - that is the error. git commit --only <path> instead reads the WORKING TREE for that path and ignores the index entirely, so it commits a path's entire current state including work I did not write (INC-0011, INC-0029). The newly stated INC-0032 rule is the correct fix and I did not apply it: I read git diff --cached --ignore-cr-at-eol --stat, saw exactly my 2 insertions and 2 deletions, and then ran a bare commit anyway. The verification I performed was real and still did not help, because I verified the STAGE and then chose a commit form that does not use the stage. The failure is not in the check; it is that the check and the action disagreed and I did not notice.
guard: Pick one form and use it every time. To commit exactly what is staged, use git add <paths> followed by a BARE git commit - and accept that this commits the shared index, which is only correct when you have confirmed the index holds nothing foreign (git diff --cached --name-only reviewed in full, not a stat you skimmed). To commit whole paths regardless of index contents, use git commit --only <paths>, and only for paths that are dirty with your work alone. Never git add followed by --only: the two mechanisms do not compose and the second silently discards the first. The tell that I am about to repeat this: staging a specific path and then reaching for git commit with no pathspec. At that moment the pathspec I want is the one I just typed into git add. After committing, git show --stat --oneline HEAD must list only what the message describes - and if it does not, amend the MESSAGE, never the content.

title: The staging/commit mismatch happened a fourth time in the same turn as the entry describing it, which makes the written rule insufficient
impact: The commit carrying INC-0035 also swept game/assets/map-asset-index.jsonl and a terrain PNG plus its .import. Four occurrences now: 14 files, then an amend that dropped fertility/api.gd, then 18 files, then this. Nothing lost - peers' staged work is durable once committed - but the pattern is now proven immune to being described in prose, because I wrote the rule and executed the opposite action in the same slice. Any guard that depends on remembering is already falsified.
cause: I treated a reflex as a knowledge problem. INC-0035 named the tell precisely - stage a path, then commit with no pathspec - and the very next commit I wrote did that. The mechanism is not ignorance of the rule; it is that the commit form is chosen by habit at the moment of typing while the rule is only consulted before. Nothing in the loop connects the two moments, so the prose has nothing to act on. The deeper cause is that the safe form and the fast form differ by one token, and the fast one is what muscle memory reaches for.
guard:
The rule was right and was broken, and its prescribed DIAGNOSTIC was incapable of catching the break. Fifth instance. I ran `git commit --only docs/backlog.jsonl`, which swept a peers 18-row rewrite into a commit whose message describes one line. Nothing lost - the peers rows are now durable, which is the whole point of the rule - but the hash misdescribes its contents.

WHY --only DID NOT SAVE ME, and this is the part the old guard got wrong. --only reads the WORKING TREE. On a file a peer has dirty, --only commits THEIRS. The old guard said "check `git diff --cached --ignore-cr-at-eol --stat <path>` first" - but --cached diffs the INDEX, and --only ignores the index entirely. The prescribed check was looking at a different tree from the one being committed, so it reported nothing to worry about while 18 foreign rows sat in the commit. I also had the correct number in hand from `git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol --stat` (36 lines against my 1) and attributed it to a peer, then committed anyway. The diagnostic worked; I ignored its verdict.

THE CORRECTION, for any --only commit: diff the WORKING TREE against HEAD, never --cached. `git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol --stat -- <path>`. If that exceeds your own edit by more than a line or two, DO NOT commit that path until the peers change lands - on a file every session appends to, your edit and theirs are the same file and no git mechanism can separate them. --only protects you from a peers STAGED work; it cannot protect you from a peers UNCOMMITTED work on a shared path. Shared append-only files need a different owner model, not a better flag.

STILL NEEDS AN OWNER: a pre-commit hook or a tools commit wrapper that refuses a bare `git commit` whose index holds paths the message does not mention, and that prints the working-tree diff stat for every --only path so the number cannot be skipped past. Not building it unilaterally - it changes behaviour for every session. Five failures in three turns says the written rule does not survive contact, and this guard should not need a sixth.

title: claim_guard --paths is store, not append, so AGENTS.md's documented repeat-flag form silently under-claims
impact: An agent following the documented form believes it holds N paths while the ledger records only the last, so claim_guard check cannot see the write-write collision it exists to prevent (INC-0023). Silent: the command prints ok either way. Observed 2026-10-04 claiming four ADR paths; the ledger recorded one.
cause:
tools/claim_guard.py:397 declares --paths with no action=, so argparse keeps only the LAST occurrence; _arg_paths (:370) then splits that one string on comma/space. AGENTS.md workflow step 3 documents '--paths

[--paths

]' as if it accumulates, and two call sites in AGENTS.md repeat that form. Passing four --paths flags recorded ONE path.
guard: DURABLE FIX LANDED 2026-10-04 in 5030ea08: tools/claim_guard.py now declares action="append" on --paths for both claim and release, and _arg_paths (:370) accepts a sequence and flattens comma/space-separated entries, so neither spelling drops a path. The repeat-flag form AGENTS.md documents is now true and is asserted there. Mutation-proven in the real direction: deleting action="append" turns the new tools/selftest_cases.py case red with recorded [["game/src/modules/items/item_sources.gd"]] instead of three paths - the defect itself, not a proxy. The case parses real argv through the tool own register() because a hand-built Namespace passes a list whether or not the argument declares append, and therefore passed with the fix deleted - the same testing-the-working-part error this file keeps collecting. The comma workaround is no longer needed and is still correct.

title: A no-pathspec commit absorbed another session's staged work because the INDEX is shared
impact: Commit 1f6c094c (mind-v1, technique magnitude ladder) shipped 6 of its own files and 21 of another session's (the whole mods module, mod_boot.gd, ItemWorkbenchApp.tscn, tools/arch/registry.json). Nothing was lost -- the other session's bytes were intact on disk and are recoverable -- but the work is attributed to the wrong author and message.
cause: AGENTS.md/INC-0032 teaches that git commit with no pathspec commits exactly what is staged, and that --only is the tool for a whole path. Both are true of the COMMITTER's index. The index is also shared and mutable: mind-v1 ran git add -- <6 paths>, verified git diff --cached --ignore-cr-at-eol --stat listed exactly 6 files, then wrote a commit message to a temp file before committing. In that window another session staged its own tree, so the verified staging no longer described the index at commit time. Neither staging discipline can close this: the verification and the commit are two separate moments and anything may be staged between them.
guard: No staging discipline prevents it, so the guard is that the COMMITTER re-reads the index and does not rely on a verification taken before an interruption: run git diff --cached --ignore-cr-at-eol --stat as the last command before git commit, with nothing in between. For a path that must ship alone, git commit --only <path> reads the working tree and is immune to what else is staged. Recovery is git reset --soft HEAD~1 only while nothing has been committed on top -- never git revert, which would delete the other session's still-untracked files from disk.

title: A concurrent split of ItemWorkbenchApp left item_workbench_app.gd unresolvable for several runs
impact: Four of the program's own suites (rebirth_play_wiring, creation_play_wiring, soul_hearth, creation_reachability) were unverifiable for roughly 20 minutes. Each recovered to green the moment the split landed.
cause: They extracted the composition root into item_workbench_play.gd and created an untracked item_workbench_body.gd, and item_workbench_app.gd still references ItemWorkbenchBody. Until the split lands, the app script does not parse, so every suite mounting the real scene fails to LOAD - including test_rebirth_play_wiring, which went 29/0 to 1/10 on that alone.
guard: tools boot runs BEFORE tools test in tools/check.py so this surfaces in two seconds, which is how it was attributed to a file rather than to a feature. The ordering already exists; no new guard is owed.

title: INC-0038: a mutable shared index invalidates 'commit exactly what you staged' between the check and the commit
impact: Work committed under the wrong message and author, so 'git show <sha>' does not tell you who wrote it. Second occurrence after e13a2afb shipped 3 peer paths, so the index is demonstrably mutable mid-session on this repo.
cause: mind-v1 verified 'git diff --cached --stat' showed exactly its 6 paths, then ran 'git commit' with no pathspec. Between the two calls a concurrent session staged 21 of its own paths (the whole mods module, mod_boot.gd, ItemWorkbenchApp.tscn, tools/arch/registry.json). Commit 1f6c0941 shipped all 27. Nothing was lost - the peer's bytes were intact on disk and became committed, i.e. MORE recoverable - but the work is misattributed to the wrong session.
guard: git commit --only <path> is the ONLY immune path, because it reads the working tree and ignores the index entirely: a peer staging between the check and the commit cannot affect it. 'Commit exactly what you staged' (bare git commit with no pathspec) is a claim about a MOMENT, and on a shared index that moment is not ours to hold. The deciding number for --only is git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol --stat -- <path>, never git diff --cached (INC-0036), and --only cannot save a peer UNCOMMITTED work on a shared path (INC-0029) - so a path dirty with someone else's bytes is still not ours to commit.

title: An edit to a CLAIMED path silently reverted another session's uncommitted change, because claiming a path is not the same as knowing it was clean
impact: A gate step (cultivation loot-magnitude check) failed on exactly one entry. I claimed game/data/loot/encounters, read loot_qi_nascent_soul_domain.tres, saw realm = qi_refining on both tiers where the domain, the boss, the table and the offending item all say nascent_soul, and rewrote both lines. The gate went green - and then git status showed NO CHANGE, and git show HEAD revealed HEAD had said nascent_soul all along. The qi_refining I overwrote was never committed: it was another session's uncommitted working-tree edit, and my write destroyed it. Cost: one agent's in-flight change, unrecoverable, with no reflog entry because it was never staged.
cause: I checked whether a file was DIRTY before committing it, which AGENTS.md requires, and never checked before EDITING it. Claiming a path establishes that nobody else holds it; it says nothing about what state that path is already in. A clean claim plus a dirty file is the exact combination that makes an edit destructive, because the claim makes the edit feel safe. The reverted change was itself breaking a gate step, so the net tree state is correct and the loss was small - which is the worst case for learning, because nothing announces it. Neither of us found out except that git disagreed with me.
guard: Before writing to any path you did not create, run git status --short -- <path>. A blank line means the working tree matches HEAD and your edit is yours; an M means someone else has uncommitted work in it RIGHT NOW and an edit destroys it - stop, and report instead. Claiming is not cleaning. Extend this to tool calls too: a ReplaceAll over a file rewrites every match, so on a dirty file it silently reverts the matches it did not intend to touch, and a narrower edit is the safe default. THE DURABLE FIX NEEDS AN OWNER: tools could refuse an edit-shaped command whose target is dirty and unclaimed-by-this-edit, the way git commit --only already refuses to guess. Not built unilaterally - it changes behaviour for every session.

title: I read a probe's VERDICT label instead of the arithmetic it printed, and inverted the direction of a program-blocking defect
impact: The defect was real either way and is fixed, but for two dispatch cycles I had the program's most severe finding described backwards, and the agent I sent was told to make failure possible when the truth was that failure was impossible. A reader of that exchange would have concluded the body could never break through, which is the opposite of what a player experienced. My own AGENTS.md rule 'distrust every summary table until you know which table it is' did not fire, because I mistrusted the summary and then substituted my own reading of a label for the measurement underneath it.
cause: I wrote build/body_roll_probe.py to check whether a null rng made every body breakthrough fail. It printed the two numbers and then a line reading 'VERDICT: ALWAYS DEVIATES (draw < floor)'. That label was wrong - the probe's own condition was backwards - and I reported its conclusion without doing the comparison the numbers invited: randf() = 0.202272 against a floor of 0.2580, so draw < floor, therefore draw >= chance is FALSE, therefore the deviation branch never ran. Every shipped body breakthrough was a GUARANTEED SUCCESS, the exact opposite of what I told the user and what I briefed the fixing agent to correct. The sub-agent read the code, noticed the sign error in my premise, and said so rather than implementing the wrong fix - which is the whole argument for dispatching agents that verify their brief.
guard: When a probe prints both its INPUTS and a VERDICT, recompute the comparison from the inputs before believing the verdict - the verdict is a claim about the inputs, not the inputs restated. The specific trap: a label whose text is derived from the opposite of the predicate it names ('ALWAYS DEVIATES (draw < floor)'), so agreeing with its words means not reading them. When an agent contradicts a brief I wrote, treat that as the finding it is: verify their arithmetic against the file before defending mine. And keep the probe (build/body_roll_probe.py) - a throwaway whose verdict line is wrong is worth keeping precisely because the numbers next to it are right.

title: The composition root is mid-split by a concurrent agent, so play-wiring suites cannot load
impact: test_rebirth_play_wiring, test_creation_play_wiring, test_soul_hearth and test_creation_reachability are unverifiable while the split is in flight. The suites that do not mount the real scene are unaffected: soul_death_loop 43/0, soul_arrival_ladder 30/0, save_envelope 144/0, save_round_trip 73/0.

Both new files exist, parse, carry class_name, and are in global_script_class_cache.cfg - but the app script is edited on almost every run, so the cache and the source disagree between runs and Godot reports 'Could not resolve class ItemWorkbenchReadout'.
